description: We are QUANTARA, a student team exploring how science and technology can help people understand safety challenges. Through FLARE, we make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to find, compare and interpret. We combine scientific questions, interactive design and AI-assisted development, while distinguishing published evidence from interpretations and future ideas.
summary:
FLARE is a browser-based dashboard that helps users find, compare and interpret NASA microgravity combustion research. Built by Team QUANTARA for Flame in Freefall, it combines an atlas of 21 investigations with 13 Saffire test records transcribed from a NASA publication. Users can rank investigations for different habitats, compare experimental conditions, explore compatible CSV data and examine hypothetical scenarios. 
An offline screening heuristic displays a hazard level alongside its assumptions and evidence limits. Optional AI assistance through OpenRouter explains the project data and assesses scenarios with source identifiers. FLARE connects published research, experimental similarity and questions about spacecraft fire safety in one interface. It supports learning and research exploration; it is not a validated fire simulation or an operational safety system. Raw PSI integration, partial-gravity validation and a proposed suppression-agent recovery concept remain future work.
details:
FLARE grew from a practical question: how can someone find relevant combustion research, compare experimental conditions and understand what changes when conditions differ from expectations? Team QUANTARA developed a browser-based dashboard for the Flame in Freefall challenge, bringing research summaries, experimental comparisons and optional AI interpretation into one interface.

The investigation atlas contains 21 combustion-related investigations. Users can rank them for crewed spacecraft, space stations, lunar or Martian bases and pressurized rovers, and compare up to three side by side. The ranking exposes six relevance factors and their weights; these are project design choices, not validated measures of safety. Some data-access details remain explicitly marked for verification.

The numerical library contains 13 Saffire test records manually transcribed from Table 1 of NASA NTRS document 20180005168. It preserves source notes and missing outcomes rather than replacing them with zero. These are published conditions and selected results, not raw PSI measurements or recorded time series. Users can filter and download records or load a compatible CSV. The DNA comparison treats experimental conditions as a fingerprint, using equal-weight normalized distances over selected comparable fields, with at least four shared features. Similarity indicates comparable recorded conditions, not equivalent fire behaviour. Numeric profiles and scatter plots support descriptive exploration.

Run Experiment starts from a Saffire record and lets users change material, oxygen, pressure, airflow, flow direction and gravity. A transparent offline heuristic displays five hazard levels with explanatory drivers and evidence-coverage notes. Symbolic flame graphics illustrate regimes rather than simulate combustion. Nearby-run growth charts use published average spread rates to draw idealized lines; they are not measured flame trajectories. A connected AI can add a short assessment and an explanation grounded in the supplied project context. FLARE checks source identifiers and equipment identifiers, but those checks do not establish that every AI claim is correct.

The application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG, with Python scripts for data preparation and an optional local server. Its local tools work without a server when the accompanying files are retained. Offline assistance uses keyword retrieval. Online assistance uses OpenRouter and requires internet access and user authorization or an API key.

Our creative contribution is the connection between an experimental fingerprint, habitat-specific research ranking and scenario exploration, while keeping published observations separate from interpretations and hypothetical conditions. The intended benefit is clearer access to research for students and people exploring spacecraft fire safety. The interface also introduces Earth applications of the cited NASA research; FLARE itself has not demonstrated an improvement in fire protection.

The screening heuristic is unvalidated, and its material thresholds and coefficients include approximate assumptions. Pressure is displayed and supplied to AI but does not affect the local hazard score; the Saffire table provides no pressure or fuel-temperature measurements. The numerical library contains only microgravity runs, so lunar, Martian and Earth scenarios cannot be treated as validated predictions. AI answers can be wrong, and service availability varies. FLARE provides neither certified risk assessment nor emergency procedures.

Future work includes traceable raw PSI data, better-supported material parameters and validation against suitable experiments, including partial-gravity data if available. Separately, we would like to investigate containment or recovery of extinguishing material after suppression. This is an untested research concept, not an implemented FLARE feature or a demonstrated device.

To open the downloadable project, download the ZIP file from Google Drive and extract all files into one folder. Open index.html from the extracted folder in a desktop web browser such as Chrome or Edge. Keep all accompanying files and subfolders together; do not open index.html from inside the ZIP or use Google Drive's preview to run the application. No installation, Python or .bat file is required for the local tools. These tools and the local assistant can be used offline. Optional online AI features require internet access and your own OpenRouter API key, entered under SI assistant > AI engine.
